blocks.text: Job uses the same simile, but in a different context, Iob. IX, 26. They have passed by [col. 171] (my days) like ships אבה ebe, as the eagle flies to its food. In these words, to say this in passing, I suspect with Selomo and others that Ebe is the name of a river, because even today there are two rivers named ابى [Abī] Ebe or Ebbe in those regions: one of them is near Kufa, the other in the district of Babylonia called Wasit, which is the Mesene of the Greeks. See the Lexicon of the distinguished Golius, p. 2. Something else could also be adduced. In Arabic ابى [abā] aba is a verb meaning to gird oneself for a journey. So אניות אבה, ships ebe, could be called swift ships, girded for a journey, or actuariae [light vessels], if you prefer, which are the more nimble ^{(1)}. Thus the spans of our swiftly running life are compared both with ships of this kind and with the birds we have mentioned, that [II, 752] is, with eagles hastening to their food. This is not only because the speed is equal in both cases, but also because nothing remains of time once it has slipped away, just as the eagle in the air and the ship in the sea leave no trace of themselves, as Solomon observes, Prov. XXX, 19. Hence in Sap. V, 10. 11. 12. the author of the book, whoever he is, elegantly uses both similes to teach that we, scarcely born, at once so fail that nothing is left of the life we have lived.

Now another point must be observed in the flight of eagles: it is not only swift but also sustained. For the eagle does not tire quickly, but, when the situation demands, flies for a very long time and travels to quite distant places. Hence the poets imagine that two eagles, sent out by Jupiter, one from the farthest east and the other from the farthest west, did not cease from flight until they met at Delphi, or on neighbouring Parnassus. See Pindar, Pyth. 4, and the Scholiast there, Strabo, book 9, Plutarch, De Orac., and Claudian's Prologue to the Panegyric of Manlius Theodorus. Of the same kind is the fiction of the Arabs in Damiri: وهو اشد الطير طيرانا واقوي جناحا حتي انه ليطير ما بين المشرق والمغرب في يوم واحد [wa-huwa ashadd al-ṭayr ṭayarānan wa-aqwā janāḥan ḥattā annahu la-yaṭīru mā bayna al-mashriq wa-al-maghrib fī yawm wāḥid] It is of all birds the most vigorous in flight and has the strongest wings, so that it flies across all that lies between east and west in a single day. Accordingly Scripture applies eagle's wings to those who are carried far away. Thus in Apoc. XII, 14. the woman, who is the church, is given two wings of a great eagle, with which to fly into the desert out of the serpent's sight. And in Psalm. CXXXIX, 9. the Syriac translator has: If I raise my wings ܐܝܟ ܕܢܫܪܐ, like an eagle, and dwell in the uttermost sea. And the Arabic: If I were lifted up on two wings كالنسر [ka-al-nasr] like an eagle, so as to come to the ends of the sea. The Ethiopic also: If I take my wings ከመ ፡ ንስር ፡ like an eagle, etc. Yet the Hebrew does not have כנפי נשר, wings of an eagle, but כנפי שחר, wings of the dawn. This is followed by the Greeks, the Chaldee, the Vulgate translator, Jerome and all the Hebrews. Here also belongs the statement in Proverb. XXIII, 5. that fleeting riches take on the wings of an eagle, with which they fly off into heaven, that is, they slip away very swiftly and are removed far from you, so that they are no longer in your possession. Hence in Lucian's Timon Plutus, the god of riches, says that he limps and advances only slowly when he is sent by Jupiter to someone to increase his wealth. Ὁπόταν δὲ ἀπαλλάττεσθαι δέῃ [Hopotan de apallattesthai deē], he says, πτηνὸν ὄψει πολὺ τῶν ὀρνέων ὠκύτερον [ptēnon opsei poly tōn orneōn ōkyteron]· But when I must depart, you will see me winged, far swifter than birds. So, since God says in Exod. XIX, 4. that he carried the Israelites, as they went out of Egypt, as on eagles' wings, the Jews infer from this that they covered 120 miles in one hour from Rameses to Succoth. So R. Selomo on Exod. XII, 37.: מרעמסס סכתה מאה ועשרים מיל היו ובאו שם לפי שעה שנ״ ואשא אתכם על כנפי [col. 172] [II, 753] נשרים, From Rameses to Succoth is a journey of one hundred and twenty miles, which they covered in the space of one hour, as it is said: “And I will carry them on eagles' wings”.
Nor should this be omitted: there is no bird that rises higher than the eagle ^{(2)}. Hence in the oracle given concerning the Athenians,
Αἰετὸς ἐν νεφέλῃσι γενήσεαι, — — [Aietos en nephelēsi genēseai, — —]
